note.note:
History:
- Chief complaint: Shortness of breath with wheeze and cough for 2–3 days.
- Onset/trigger: Began during a run when patient became unusually short of breath; now occurs with brisk walking. Not clearly at rest.
- Progression: Persistent over last 2–3 days; minimal relief with blue inhaler.
- Associated symptoms: Wheeze, cough. Denies sputum production.
- Prior control: Asthma reportedly well controlled until current episode.
- Previous episodes: Last asthma attack ~3–4 years ago.
- Monitoring: Usual peak flow approximately 380 L/min (per patient agreement with clinician prompt). No peak flow measured during current symptoms.

Past Medical History:
- Conditions: Asthma; hay fever. Possible eczema (patient suspects; not formally confirmed).
- Hospitalizations for asthma: None reported.
- Prior oral steroids for asthma: Never.
- Last asthma review: ~2 years ago.
- Family history: Brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Allergies: No medication allergies reported.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (blue reliever inhaler) used as needed; also using morning and evening prophylactically; dose/route/frequency not fully documented.
  - Preventer inhaler: Patient uses a twice-daily preventer; name unclear. Clinician references “brown Clenil” (beclomethasone) and discusses dosing; dose not clearly documented. Conflict noted (see Quality checks).
  - Cetraben (emollient) for skin; dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Hydrocortisone (topical) for skin; dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Bactroban (mupirocin) was mentioned once by patient but later not confirmed. Conflict noted.

Physical Examination:
- Not performed (telehealth visit).
- No vital signs documented.
- Symptom negatives: No sputum production reported.

Impression:
- Mild asthma exacerbation over 2–3 days with exercise-induced dyspnea, wheeze, and cough; suboptimal response to reliever inhaler.

Management Plan:
- Increase preventer inhaler (brown Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review.
- Continue salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed up to every 2–4 hours; frequent need (e.g., every 2 hours) indicates poor control and need for urgent reassessment.
- Arrange face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for chest examination and peak flow measurement.
- Safety net: If breathing worsens or reliever is needed very frequently, go to the emergency department without waiting for the appointment.
- Possible treatments at visit depending on findings: Oral steroids and/or antibiotics (to be decided after examination).

Patient Summary:
- Patient with known asthma developed shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough over 2–3 days, triggered by exertion and not relieved by the blue inhaler.
- Clinician suspects a mild asthma exacerbation. Preventer dose increased temporarily, and urgent in-person assessment arranged with guidance to seek emergency care if symptoms escalate.

Key Takeaways:
- Increase brown preventer (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily.
- Use blue inhaler as needed up to every 2–4 hours; if needing it that often or symptoms worsen, seek emergency care.
- Book and attend a face-to-face appointment in the next few days for examination and peak flow testing.

Next Steps:
- Face-to-face GP visit within a few days for chest exam and peak flow readings.
- Consider need for oral steroids and/or antibiotics after assessment.
- Reassess asthma control and inhaler regimen at the visit.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vital signs, objective respiratory exam, current peak flow during symptoms, complete and confirmed medication list with doses/routes/frequencies, smoking status, spacer use/technique, vaccination status, confirmed eczema diagnosis.
- Internal conflicts:
  - Preventer inhaler identity: Patient initially stated the preventer is “blue” (typically a reliever), while clinician referenced “brown Clenil” as preventer; preventer name/dose not clearly documented.
  - Medications: Patient first mentioned “Salbutamol, Flanel, Bactroban, Hydrocortisone,” then later “Cetraben and Hydrocortisone.” Unclear whether Bactroban is current; “Flanel” is unclear. Conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally understandable but with several unclear/inaudible segments and missing drug names; some clinician prompts completed by assumption and patient assent.
